topics.title: Probability Problem (I made up)
topics.text:
Gary is playing a carnival game in which he is pulling marbles from a box. Each marble is red or green, and Gary gets to pull a marble five times without replacement. He wins if he pulls four or more green marbles. There are 20 red marbles and 10 green marbles in the box. However, three pulls in, Gary gets a call from his friend. If Gary has pulled two or more green marbles up to this point, the carnival man will replace 5 of the remaining green marbles with red marbles. After Gary finishes talking, he will finish his last two pulls. What is the probability that Gary wins?



Hint 1:

Click to reveal hidden textThe fact that the carnival man will replace the marbles only if Gary has pulled two or more green marbles in three pulls is unnecessary, since if Gary has pulled 0 or 1 marbles in his first three pulls, he can't win.




Hint 2:

Click to reveal hidden textSplit it up into cases. Gary could pull two or three marbles in the first three pulls.




Hint 3:

Click to reveal hidden textIf Gary pulls three marbles, we need extra cases, since Gary could pull one or two green marbles in the last two pulls and still win.

topics.title: Just a Quick "Common Sense" Question(s)
topics.text:
So basically I've encountered a lot of these problems where they give you proportions like 4 birds eats 4 worms in 4 minutes. How many minutes does it take 32 birds to eat 32 worms? At a quick glance, it's obviously that the answer is 4 minutes since for both of them the amount of birds equal the amount of worms. Though my teacher would make us explain and doesn't accept common sense reasoning(trust me, I've tried it and got 1/2 of the test marked off, aka automatic F) so I put 1 bird would eat 1 worm in 4 minutes (basically simplest form), and then convert it to 32 birds eat 32 worms in 4 minutes. Again, I got marked off because she said her way was more time-conserving which is $4 birds/4 worms * 4 minutes = 32 birds/32 worms * y minutes$. Then, we would solve for "y" to get the answer. What is the logic to her formula?



Thanks.

angrypidgeot

topics.title: AMC 8 Problem
topics.text:
2007 AMC 8 #13

Sets $A$ and $B$, shown in the Venn diagram, have the same number of elements. Their union has $2007$ elements and their intersection has $1001$ elements. Find the number of elements in $A$.



IMAGE

$\mathrm{(A)}\ 503 \qquad \mathrm{(B)}\ 1006 \qquad \mathrm{(C)}\ 1504 \qquad \mathrm{(D)}\ 1507 \qquad \mathrm{(E)}\ 1510$



Solution:

Let $x$ be the number of elements in $A$ and $B$.

Since the union is the sum of all elements in $A$ and $B$,

and $A$ and $B$ have the same number of elements then,

$2x-1001 = 2007$

$2x = 3008$

$x = 1504$.

The answer is $\boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 1504}$



I understand that the answer is written on the website, but can someone explain to me why we use 2x Wouldn't the sum of A and B be just x? Can someone just explain why each step is what it is or suggest an alternate way to do this?



Thanks,

-Ericafp

topics.title: Combinatorics Problem
topics.text:
The Jones family has 5 boys & 3 girls, and 2 of the girls are twins. In how many ways can they be seated in a row of 8 chairs if the twins insist on sitting together, and their other sister refuses to sit next to either of her sisters?





This was the answer I found online:





If the twins sit at the end of the row, then the other sister can sit at one of 5 places so that she’s not next to the twins. 1st choose one of the 2 ends (2 choices) and seat the 2 twins (2! choices); then seat the other sister (5 choices); then seat the remaining 5 brothers (5! choices).

2! X 2! X 5! X 5! = 2400 ways





But it doesn't mention in the problem that the boys have to be seated always adjacent to each other...so that means I'm assuming you can have a configuration like this:



BTBGBBB



T representing the two girls...



My calculation was as follows...



2! * 7 ways to place the twins in the 8 seats.



in (2!*5) of those configurations you have 4 places to place the other girl, so (2!*5)*4 = 40.



in (2!*2) - the ends of the row - we have 5 places to place the other girl, so (2!*2)*5 = 20.



5! ways to place the boys in any of these configs, so (40+20)*5! = 7200.



Is this correct or incorrect?

topics.title: Casework problems without Burnsides
topics.text:
Hello,



I have seen a plethora of problems that are generally solved using casework, but many people have been using Burnside's Lemma to basically trivialize them. I, personally like a casework approach better, so I have stuck to that. Unfortunately, when I solve these types of problems, I usually miss a case, over/under count, or do something to where I miss the problem.



Here are some examples:



How many ways can you color the vertices of a square with 6 different colors, if rotations and reflections are the same?



How many ways can you color a 6 sector spinner with 4 different colors, if rotations are the same?



How many ways can you color the vertices of a cube with 5 different colors, if rotation and reflections are the same?



Like I said early, I would appreciate it if there were no Burnside's solutions, but more casework solutions, and how to basically approach the problems in general.



Thanks!
